Travelling wave solutions of the generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation

Journal: Chaos, Solitons & Fractals
P. G. Estévez Address: Departamento de Física Fundamental, Área de Física Teórica, Universidad de Salamanca, 37008 Salamanca, Spain    Ş. Kuru Corresponding author: On leave of absence from: Department of Physics, Faculty of Science, Ankara University 06100 Ankara, Turkey.    J. Negro Email: jnegro@fta.uva.es    L. M. Nieto Address: Departamento de Física Teórica, Atómica y Óptica, Universidad de Valladolid, 47071 Valladolid, Spain
Abstract

A class of particular travelling wave solutions of the generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation is studied systematically using the factorization technique. Then, the general travelling wave solutions of Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation, and of its modified version, are also recovered.
Pacs:05.45.Yv, 52.35.Mw, 52.35.Sb, 02.30.Jr

, and

1 Introduction

The generalized BBM (Benjamin-Bona-Mahony) equation has a higher order nonlinearity of the form

ut+ux+a​un​ux+ux​x​t=0,n≥1,u_{t}+u_{x}+a\,u^{n}\,u_{x}+u_{xxt}=0,\quad n\geq 1, (1)

where aa is constant. The case n=1n=1 corresponds to the BBM equation

ut+ux+a​u​ux+ux​x​t=0,u_{t}+u_{x}+a\,u\,u_{x}+u_{xxt}=0, (2)

which was first proposed in 1972 by Benjamin et al [1]. This equation is an alternative to the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation, and describes the unidirectional propagation of small-amplitude long waves on the surface of water in a channel. The BBM equation is not only convenient for shallow water waves but also for hydromagnetic waves, acoustic waves, and therefore it has more advantages compared with the KdV equation. When n=2n=2, Eq.(1) is called the modified BBM equation

ut+ux+a​u2​ux+ux​x​t=0.u_{t}+u_{x}+a\,u^{2}\,u_{x}+u_{xxt}=0. (3)

When looking for travelling wave solutions, the BBM and modified BBM equations can be reduced to ordinary differential equations that possess the Painlevé property and which are integrable in terms of elliptic functions [2, 3]. The generalized BBM equation is also integrable in terms of elliptic functions, provided that some restrictions on the parameters are imposed. Recently many methods have been presented to obtain the travelling wave solutions of the generalized BBM equation: the tanh-sech and the sine-cosine methods [4, 5], an approach based on balancing principle to obtain some explicit solutions in terms of elliptic function [6], and an extended algebraic method with symbolic computation [7].

Our aim is to investigate systematically the travelling wave solutions of these equations, applying the factorization technique [8, 9]. Thus, we will get all the previously known solutions and some new ones, supplying a new general approach. Assuming that the generalized BBM equation has an exact solution in the form of a travelling wave, then it will reduce to a third order ordinary differential equation (ODE). This equation can be integrated trivially to a second order ODE, which can be factorized in two ways: the first one by means of differential operators and the second one by using a first integral (that can also be factorized in terms of first integrals). These factorizations give rise to the same first order ODE that provides the travelling wave solutions of the nonlinear equation. This first order ODE for n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 is integrable, but for other values of nn, we can also find some particular solutions by imposing some restrictions on the parameters.

The paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we introduce the factorization technique for nonlinear equations, and we show how to apply it to find the travelling wave solutions of the generalized BBM equation. In section 3, we consider some special cases to get particular solutions of generalized BBM. In section 4, we obtain the solutions of the BBM and modified BBM. Finally, section 5 ends the paper with some conclusions. In the Appendix, we give also some useful information about the elliptic functions that are used in the previous sections.

2 Travelling waves of the generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation

2.1 Travelling wave solutions

Let us assume that Eq. (1) has an exact solution in the form of a travelling wave

u⁡(x,t)=ϕ⁡(ξ),ξ=h​x−ω​t,u(x,t)=\phi(\xi),\quad\xi=h\,x-\omega\,t, (4)

where hh and ω\omega are real constants. If we substitute (4) in Eq. (1), we get

−h2​ω​ϕξ​ξ​ξ+(h−ω)​ϕξ+h​a​ϕn​ϕξ=0.-h^{2}\,\omega\,\phi_{\xi\xi\xi}+(h-\omega)\phi_{\xi}+h\,a\,\phi^{n}\,\phi_{\xi}=0. (5)

After integrating with respect to ξ\xi, we have

ϕξ​ξ−h−ωh2​ω​ϕ−a(n+1)​h​ω​ϕn+1=−R,\phi_{\xi\xi}-\frac{h-\omega}{h^{2}\,\omega}\,\phi-\frac{a}{(n+1)\,h\,\omega}\,\phi^{n+1}=-R, (6)

where RR is an integration constant. Let us introduce the following linear transformation of the dependent and independent variables

ξ=h​θ,ϕ⁡(ξ)=(c⁡(n+1)a)1/n​W​(θ)\xi=h\,\theta,\quad\phi(\xi)=\left(\frac{c\,(n+1)}{a}\right)^{1/n}W(\theta) (7)

where θ=x−c​t\theta=x-c\,t and c=ω/hc={\omega}/{h}. In this way (6) becomes the nonlinear second order ODE

d2​Wd​θ2−Wn+1−k​W=D,\frac{d^{2}W}{d\theta^{2}}-W^{n+1}-k\,W=D, (8)

where the new constants are

k=1−cc,D=−R​h2​(ac⁡(n+1))1/n.k=\frac{1-c}{c},\quad D={-R\,h^{2}}\left(\frac{a}{c\,(n+1)}\right)^{1/n}. (9)

Therefore, if we are interested in finding the travelling wave solutions of (1), we have to solve the ODE (8).

2.2 Factorization of some special type of nonlinear second order ODE

In this section we will introduce a factorization technique applied to nonlinear second order ODE of the special form

d2​Wd​θ2−β​d​Wd​θ+F⁡(W)=0,\frac{d^{2}W}{d\theta^{2}}-\beta\frac{dW}{d\theta}+F(W)=0, (10)

where F⁡(W)F(W) is an arbitrary function of WW and β\beta is constant. This equation can be factorized as

[dd​θ−f2​(W,θ)]​[dd​θ−f1​(W,θ)]​W​(θ)=0\left[\frac{d}{d\theta}-f_{2}(W,\theta)\right]\left[\frac{d}{d\theta}-f_{1}(W,\theta)\right]W(\theta)=0 (11)

being f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} two unknown functions that may depend explicitly on WW and θ\theta. In order to find f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, we expand (11)

d2​Wd​θ2\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}W}{d\theta^{2}} −\displaystyle- (f1+f2+∂f1∂W​W)​d​Wd​θ+f1​f2​W−W​∂f1∂θ=0,\displaystyle\left(f_{1}+f_{2}+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial W}\ W\right)\frac{dW}{d\theta}+f_{1}\,f_{2}\,W-W\ \frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial\theta}=0, (12)

and then comparing with (10), we obtain the following consistency conditions

f1​f2=FW+∂f1∂θ,f_{1}f_{2}=\frac{F}{W}+\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial\theta}, (13)
f2+∂(W​f1)∂W=β.f_{2}+\frac{\partial(Wf_{1})}{\partial W}=\beta. (14)

If we find a solution for this factorization problem, it will allow us to write a compatible first order ODE

[dd​θ−f1​(W,θ)]​W​(θ)=0\left[\frac{d}{d\theta}-f_{1}(W,\theta)\right]W(\theta)=0 (15)

that provides a (particular) solution [8, 9] to the nonlinear ODE (10). In the applications of this paper f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} will depend only on WW.

2.3 Factorization of the generalized BBM equation

When we apply the factorization technique described above to Eq. (8), then we have β=0\beta=0, F⁡(W)=−Wn+1−k​W−DF(W)=-W^{n+1}-k\,W-D, and the consistency conditions given by (13) and (14) take the form

f1​f2=−Wn−k−D​W−1,f_{1}f_{2}=-W^{n}-k-D\,W^{-1}, (16)
f2=−f1−W​∂f1∂W.f_{2}=-f_{1}-W\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial W}. (17)

Substituting (17) in (16) we get

W​f1​∂f1∂W+f12−Wn−k−D​W−1=0.Wf_{1}\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial W}+f_{1}^{2}-W^{n}-k-D\,W^{-1}=0. (18)

The solutions of this equation are

f1=±2​Wnn+2+k+2​DW+CW2,f_{1}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2\,W^{n}}{n+2}+k+\frac{2\,D}{W}+\frac{C}{W^{2}}}, (19)

where CC is an integration constant. By replacing f1f_{1} given by (19) in Eq. (15), we have the first order ODE

d​Wd​θ∓2​Wn+2n+2+k​W2+2​D​W+C=0.\frac{dW}{d\theta}\mp\sqrt{\frac{2\,W^{n+2}}{n+2}+k\,W^{2}+2\,D\,W+C}=0. (20)

As we have already mentioned, when we solve this equation, we get also a particular solution of (8).

In the special case of the generalized BBM equation, another way to get this result is as follows: if Eq. (8) is multiplied by 2​W′2\,W^{\prime} and integrated, we arrive to

[d​Wd​θ−2​Wn+2n+2+k​W2+2​D​W+C0]\displaystyle\left[\frac{dW}{d\theta}-\sqrt{\frac{2\,W^{n+2}}{n+2}+k\,W^{2}+2\,D\,W+C_{0}}\right]
×[d​Wd​θ+2​Wn+2n+2+k​W2+2​D​W+C0]=0\displaystyle\times\left[\frac{dW}{d\theta}+\sqrt{\frac{2\,W^{n+2}}{n+2}+k\,W^{2}+2\,D\,W+C_{0}}\right]=0

which is equivalent to (20). Remark that the last equation is a product of functions, while the factorization (11) is a product of operators.

These factorizations are valid for any value of the parameters (k,nk,n) and the integration constants (C,DC,D). However, the integrability of this equation is obtained, in general, only if some constraints are imposed. As a result, it can be said that the factorization does not imply the integrability of a nonlinear equation, but can produce some solutions, under certain parameter restrictions (to be determined later, when solving Eq. (20)).

If we want to guarantee the integrability of (20), the powers of WW have to be integer numbers between 00 and 44, and therefore n∈{−1,0,1,2}n\in\{-1,0,1,2\} [3]. [Nevertheless, recall that an initial assumption on the generalized BBM equation (1) is n≥1n\geq 1.] On the other side, equation (8) has the Painlevé property only if the same condition on nn is satisfied [3]. In these cases Eq. (8) is integrable in terms of elliptic functions.

In order to find other values of nn for which it is possible to find particular solutions, let us make in Eq. (20) the transformation W=φp,p≠0,1W=\varphi^{p},p\neq 0,1, getting

(d​φd​θ)2\displaystyle\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2} =\displaystyle= 2(n+2)​p2​φ2+n​p+kp2​φ2+2​Dp2​φ2−p+Cp2​φ2−2​p.\displaystyle\frac{2}{(n+2)\,p^{2}}\varphi^{2+n\,p}+\frac{k}{p^{2}}\,\varphi^{2}+\frac{2\,D}{p^{2}}\,\varphi^{2-p}+\frac{C}{p^{2}}\,\varphi^{2-2p}. (21)

This equation is of the same type as the initial one (20), hence the same integrability conditions are valid. In this way we have the following additional cases, that will require to impose some conditions on the parameters (with n≥1n\geq 1):

  1. 1.

    If C=D=0C=D=0, then

    p∈{−2n,−1n,1n,2n}.p\in\{-\frac{2}{n},-\frac{1}{n},\frac{1}{n},\frac{2}{n}\}.

    In the next section it will be proved that p=1/np=1/n and p=2/np=2/n give the same solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) of the BBM equation (1), and therefore we consider only the case p=1/np=1/n. Then, Eq. (21) takes the form

    (d​φd​θ)2=2​n2(n+2)​φ3+k​n2​φ2.\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{2\,n^{2}}{(n+2)}\varphi^{3}+k\,n^{2}\,\varphi^{2}. (22)

    The same discussion applies for the values p=−1/np=-1/n, p=−2/np=-2/n, and choosing p=−1/np=-1/n, Eq. (21) becomes

    (d​φd​θ)2=2​n2(n+2)​φ+k​n2​φ2.\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{2\,n^{2}}{(n+2)}\varphi+k\,n^{2}\varphi^{2}. (23)
  2. 2.

    If C≠0C\neq 0 and D=0D=0, we have n=4n=4 and two possibilities: either p=1/2p=1/2 with

    (d​φd​θ)2=43​φ4+4​k​φ2+4​C​φ,\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{4}{3}\,\varphi^{4}+4\,k\,\varphi^{2}+4\,C\,\varphi, (24)

    or p=−1/2p=-{1}/{2} with

    (d​φd​θ)2=43+4​k​φ2+4​C​φ3.\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{4}{3}+4\,k\,\varphi^{2}+4\,C\,\varphi^{3}. (25)
  3. 3.

    If C=0C=0 and D≠0D\neq 0, no new solutions appear.

The solutions of equations (22)–(25) can be expressed in terms of elliptic functions. Then, using (4), (7), (9), and recalling W​(θ)=φp​(θ)W(\theta)=\varphi^{p}(\theta), the particular solution of the generalized BBM equation (1) reads

u⁡(x,t)=(c⁡(n+1)a)1/n​φp​(x−c​t).u(x,t)=\left(\frac{c\,(n+1)}{a}\right)^{1/n}\varphi^{p}(x-c\,t). (26)

The details are given in the next section.

3 Solutions of the generalized Benjamin-Bona-Mahony equation

In this section, using the basic results on elliptic functions shown in the Appendix, we will analyze the solutions of the four equations (22)–(25) obtained before, which produce particular solutions of the BBM equation.

3.1 Case C=D=0C=D=0, p=1/np={1}/{n}

In this case the third order polynomial of Eq. (22)

f⁡(φ)=2​n2(n+2)​φ3+k​n2​φ2f(\varphi)=\frac{2\,n^{2}}{(n+2)}\,\varphi^{3}+k\,n^{2}\,\varphi^{2} (27)

has two roots: φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0 (with multiplicity two) and φ0=−k(n+2)/2\varphi_{0}=-{k\,(n+2)}/{2}. When we substitute the derivatives of f⁡(φ)f(\varphi) in terms of φ0\varphi_{0} in Eq. (98), we get the following solution for Eq. (22)

φ=12​φ0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+12​n2n+2​φ02+5​k​n2​φ012​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−6​n2n+2​φ0−k​n2,\varphi=\frac{12\,\varphi_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+\frac{12\,n^{2}}{n+2}\,\varphi_{0}^{2}+5\,k\,n^{2}\varphi_{0}}{12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-\frac{6\,n^{2}}{n+2}\,\varphi_{0}-k\,n^{2}}, (28)

where the invariants are

g2=k2​n412,g3=−k3​n6216.g_{2}=\frac{k^{2}\,n^{4}}{12},\quad\quad g_{3}=-\frac{k^{3}\,n^{6}}{216}. (29)

The root φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0 gives the trivial solution, φ=0\varphi=0, and the nonzero solution of Eq. (22) can be easily found replacing φ0=−k(n+2)/2\varphi_{0}=-{k(n+2)}/{2} in (28):

φ=k⁡(n+2)4​(k​n2−12​℘​(θ,g2,g3)k​n2+6​℘​(θ,g2,g3))\varphi=\frac{k(n+2)}{4}\left(\frac{kn^{2}-12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{kn^{2}+6\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}\right) (30)

or using relation (99) in (30)

φ=2​(n+2)n2​℘​(θ+ω,g2,g3)−k⁡(n+2)6\varphi=\frac{2(n+2)}{n^{2}}\wp(\theta+\omega;g_{2},g_{3})-\frac{k\,(n+2)}{6} (31)

being ω\omega the half-period. For the values g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} of (29), the discriminant defined by (101) is equal to zero. Hence, we have both solitary wave and periodic solutions. When we use (102) in (30), we have the solitary wave solution

φ=−k⁡(n+2)2​sech2​[n2​k​θ]\varphi=-\frac{k\,(n+2)}{2}\ {\rm sech}^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{k}\,\theta\right] (32)

for 0<c<10<c<1. We get the same result by making use of (31) with the half-period ω′=(i​π/k​n)\omega^{\prime}=(i\pi/\sqrt{k}n). Using half-angle formulas for cosh⁡x\cosh x, solution (32) can also be written as

φ=−k⁡(n+2)​11+cosh⁡[n​k​θ].\varphi=-k\,(n+2)\frac{1}{1+\cosh[n\sqrt{k}\,\theta]}. (33)

When we use (103) in (30), we have the periodic solution

φ=k⁡(n+2)2​sec2⁡[n2​−k​θ]\varphi=\frac{k\,(n+2)}{2}\ \sec^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{-k}\,\theta\right] (34)

for c>1c>1. The same result can be obtained from (31) with the half-period ω=(π/−k​n)\omega=(\pi/\sqrt{-k}n). This solution can also be rewritten in the form

φ=k⁡(n+2)​11+cos⁡[n​−k​θ].\varphi=k\,(n+2)\frac{1}{1+\cos[n\,\sqrt{-k}\,\theta]}. (35)

Finally, substituting (32)–(35) in (26) and taking into account (9), we get the following solutions of Eq. (1)

u⁡(x,t)=((n+1)​(n+2)​(c−1)/a1+cosh⁡[n​1−cc​(x−c​t)])1/n=((n+1)​(n+2)​(c−1)2​a)1/n​(sech2​[n2​1−cc​(x−c​t)])1/n\begin{array}[]{ll}u(x,t)&=\displaystyle\left(\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(c-1)/a}{1+\cosh\left[n\sqrt{\frac{1-c}{c}}(x-c\,t)\right]}\right)^{\!\!1/n}\\[21.52771pt] &=\displaystyle\left(\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(c-1)}{2a}\right)^{\!\!1/n}\left({\rm sech}^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1-c}{c}}(x-c\,t)\right]\right)^{\!\!1/n}\end{array} (36)

(solitary waves) for c<1c<1, and

u⁡(x,t)=((n+1)​(n+2)​(1−c)/a1+cos⁡[n​c−1c​(x−c​t)])1/n=((n+1)​(n+2)​(1−c)2​a)1/n​(sec2⁡[n2​c−1c​(x−c​t)])1/n\begin{array}[]{ll}u(x,t)&=\displaystyle\left(\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(1-c)/a}{1+\cos\left[n\sqrt{\frac{c-1}{c}}(x-c\,t)\right]}\right)^{\!\!1/n}\\[21.52771pt] &=\displaystyle\left(\frac{(n+1)(n+2)(1-c)}{2a}\right)^{\!\!1/n}\left(\sec^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{\frac{c-1}{c}}(x-c\,t)\right]\right)^{\!\!1/n}\end{array} (37)

(periodic) for c>1c>1.

We will show now that, as it was mentioned before, by choosing in Eq. (21) p=2/np={2}/{n} instead of p=1/np={1}/{n}, we will recover the same solutions for (1). In this case, Eq. (21) becomes

(d​φd​θ)2=n22​(n+2)​φ4+k​n24​φ2\left(\frac{d\varphi}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{n^{2}}{2\,(n+2)}\ \varphi^{4}+\frac{k\,n^{2}}{4}\ \varphi^{2} (38)

and the forth order polynomial has three different roots: φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0 (with multiplicity two) and

φ0=±−k⁡(n+2)2.\varphi_{0}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{-k\,(n+2)}{2}}. (39)

From (98), the solution of Eq. (38) for each root (φ0\varphi_{0}) can be found

φ=48​φ0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+12​n2n+2​φ03+5​k​n2​φ048​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−k​n2−12​n2n+2​φ02\varphi=\frac{48\,\varphi_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+\frac{12\,n^{2}}{n+2}\,\varphi_{0}^{3}+5\,k\,n^{2}\,\varphi_{0}}{48\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-k\,n^{2}-\frac{12\,n^{2}}{n+2}\,\varphi_{0}^{2}} (40)

where the invariants are given by

g2=k2​n4192,g3=−k3​n613824.g_{2}=\frac{k^{2}\,n^{4}}{192},\quad\quad g_{3}=-\frac{k^{3}\,n^{6}}{13824}. (41)

When we choose φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0, we have again the trivial solution φ=0\varphi=0, but if we use the roots given in Eq. (39), we get the solutions of Eq. (38)

φ±=∓−k⁡(n+2)2​k​n2−48​℘​(θ,g2,g3)5​k​n2+48​℘​(θ,g2,g3).\varphi^{\pm}=\mp\sqrt{\frac{-k\,(n+2)}{2}}\frac{k\,n^{2}-48\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{5\,k\,n^{2}+48\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}. (42)

For g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} given in (41), the discriminant is equal to zero, Δ=0\Delta=0, so the Weierstrass function degenerates into trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. Then, taking into account (102) and (103), it is easy to see that the solutions (42) give rise to the same solitary wave and periodic solutions of Eq. (1) as (36) and (37).

3.2 Case C=D=0C=D=0, p=−1/np=-{1}/{n}

Here we have the second order polynomial

f⁡(φ)=2​n2(n+2)​φ+k​n2​φ2f(\varphi)=\frac{2\,n^{2}}{(n+2)}\,\varphi+k\,n^{2}\,\varphi^{2} (43)

with two roots: φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0 and

φ0=−2k⁡(n+2).\varphi_{0}=-\frac{2}{k\,(n+2)}. (44)

The expression for the solutions of (23) in terms of φ0\varphi_{0} is

φ=12​φ0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+6​n2n+2+5​k​n2​φ012​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−k​n2\varphi=\frac{12\,\varphi_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+\frac{6\,n^{2}}{n+2}+5k\,n^{2}\,\varphi_{0}}{12\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-k\,n^{2}} (45)

where the invariants are given by (29). Taking the root φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0 in (45), we get

φ=6​n212​(n+2)​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−k​n2​(n+2).\varphi=\frac{6\,n^{2}}{12(n+2)\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-k\,n^{2}(n+2)}. (46)

Since the discriminant is equal to zero for g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} given by (29), we can express the Weierstrass function in terms of trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. Thus, substituting (102) in (46), the solitary wave solution can be written

φ=−2k⁡(n+2)​sinh2​[n2​k​θ]\varphi=-\frac{2}{k\,(n+2)}\ {\rm sinh}^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{k}\,\theta\right] (47)

for c<1c<1, and using (103) in (46), we have the periodic solution

φ=2k⁡(n+2)​sin2⁡[n2​−k​θ]\varphi=\frac{2}{k\,(n+2)}\ \sin^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{-k}\,\theta\right] (48)

for c>1c>1.

When we take the second root (44) in (45), we have

φ=4​k​n2+24​℘​(θ,g2,g3)k⁡(n+2)​(k​n2−12​(n+2)​℘​(θ,g2,g3)).\varphi=\frac{4\,k\,n^{2}+24\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{k\,(n+2)(k\,n^{2}-12\,(n+2)\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3}))}.

Having in mind the degenerate cases of the Weierstrass function (shown in the Appendix), this solution can be expressed as

φ=−2k⁡(n+2)​cosh2⁡[n2​k​θ]\varphi=-\frac{2}{k\,(n+2)}\ \cosh^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{k}\,\theta\right] (49)

for c<1c<1 and

φ=2k⁡(n+2)​cos2⁡[n2​−k​θ]\varphi=\frac{2}{k\,(n+2)}\ \cos^{2}\left[\frac{n}{2}\sqrt{-k}\,\theta\right] (50)

for c>1c>1. Substituting (47)–(50) in (26) and taking into account (9), we get the solutions of Eq. (1) which were given by (36) and (37). In addition, it can be also proved that the choice p=−2/np=-{2}/{n} in Eq. (21) gives exactly the same solutions for Eq. (1).

3.3 Case C≠0C\neq 0, D=0D=0, n=4,p=1/2n=4,\,p={1}/{2}

Now the quartic polynomial

f⁡(φ)=43​φ4+4​k​φ2+4​C​φf(\varphi)=\frac{4}{3}\,\varphi^{4}+4\,k\,\varphi^{2}+4\,C\,\varphi (51)

has four roots. Substituting the first and second derivative of (51) in terms of φ0\varphi_{0} in (98), we have the general expression for the solutions

φ=3​φ0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+2​φ03+5​k​φ0+3​C3​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−2​φ02−k\varphi=\frac{3\,\varphi_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+2\,\varphi_{0}^{3}+5\,k\,\varphi_{0}+3\,C}{3\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-2\varphi_{0}^{2}-k} (52)

where the invariants are given by

g2=4​k23,g3=−8​k327−4​C23.g_{2}=\frac{4\,k^{2}}{3},\quad\quad g_{3}=-\frac{8\,k^{3}}{27}-\frac{4C^{2}}{3}. (53)

When we take the simplest root of f⁡(φ)f(\varphi), φ0=0\varphi_{0}=0, the solution of Eq. (24) is

φ=C℘⁡(θ,g2,g3)−k/3.\varphi=\frac{C}{\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-{k}/{3}}. (54)

Replacing (54) and (9) in (26), we get the particular solution of Eq. (1)

u⁡(x,t)=(5​ca​3​c​C3​c​℘​(x−c​t)+c−1)1/2.u(x,t)=\left(\sqrt{\frac{5\,c}{a}}\frac{3\,c\,C}{3\,c\,\wp(x-c\,t)+c-1}\right)^{1/2}. (55)

Using the other roots of (51) in Eq. (98), we can get the other solutions, that become trigonometric and hyperbolic, like the solutions of the case 3.1 for C=0C=0.

3.4 Case C≠0C\neq 0, D=0D=0, n=4,p=−1/2n=4,\,p=-{1}/{2}

In this case we have the third order polynomial

f⁡(φ)=4​C​φ3+4​k​φ2+43f(\varphi)=4\,C\,\varphi^{3}+4\,k\,\varphi^{2}+\frac{4}{3} (56)

has three roots. Here we will not give the roots of this polynomial, since they are a bit cumbersome. But, substituting the first and second derivative of (56) in terms of φ0\varphi_{0} in (98), we have the general expression for the solutions

φ=3​φ0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+5​k​φ0+6​C​φ023​℘​(θ,g2,g3)+3​C​φ0−k\varphi=\frac{3\,\varphi_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+5\,k\,\varphi_{0}+6\,C\,\varphi_{0}^{2}}{3\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})+3\,C\,\varphi_{0}-k} (57)

where the invariants given by (53) and the discriminant Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0.

We also notice that the choice n=4,p=−1/2n=4,\,p=-{1}/{2} gives rise to the same particular solution (55) for Eq. (1) and the other solutions can be found by the same procedure as in the above cases.

4 Solutions of the BBM and modified BBM

In this section we will consider the solutions obtained for n=1,2n=1,2 when the integration constant DD of Eq. (8) is such that D≠0D\neq 0 (to avoid confusion, in this section we will use the notation D≡DnD\equiv D_{n}, because, as we will immediately see, this constant is chosen to be dependent on nn).

First of all, let us transform Eq. (8) through the change of function W⁡(θ)=U⁡(θ)+δW(\theta)=U(\theta)+\delta into

d2​Ud​θ2−(Un+1+(n+1)!n!​Un​δ+⋯CLOSE\displaystyle\frac{d^{2}U}{d\theta^{2}}-\left(U^{n+1}+\frac{(n+1)!}{n!}U^{n}\delta+\cdots\right. (58)
OPEN+(n+1)!2​(n−1)!​Un−1​δ2+…+(n+1)!n!​U​δn)=k​U\displaystyle\quad\left.+\frac{(n+1)!}{2(n-1)!}U^{n-1}\delta^{2}+...+\frac{(n+1)!}{n!}U\delta^{n}\right)=k\,U

where the integration constant DnD_{n} has been chosen as

Dn=−k​δ−δn+1.D_{n}=-k\,\delta-\delta^{n+1}. (59)

Remark that this change of variable does not give any restriction on the solution of (8).

4.1 BBM equation (n=1n=1)

We can find the solutions of Eq. (2) when the integration constant is non-zero, D≠0D\neq 0, in Eq. (8). To do this, first we take n=1n=1 and δ≠0\delta\neq 0 in Eq. (58)

d2​Ud​θ2−U2+(2​δ−k)​U=0\frac{d^{2}U}{d\theta^{2}}-U^{2}+(2\,\delta-k)U=0 (60)

with

D1=−k​δ−δ2.D_{1}=-k\,\delta-\delta^{2}. (61)

For this case, the third order polynomial is

f⁡(U)=23​U3−(2​δ−k)​U2+C1f(U)=\frac{2}{3}U^{3}-(2\,\delta-k)U^{2}+C_{1} (62)

with three different roots. When we follow the same procedure as mentioned above, we get the solutions of the second order ODE (60) for all roots

U⁡(θ)=−5​(k−2​δ)​U0+4​U02+12​U0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)(k−2​δ)+2​U0−12​℘​(θ,g2,g3),U(\theta)=-\frac{5(k-2\,\delta)U_{0}+4\,U_{0}^{2}+12\,U_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{(k-2\,\delta)+2\,U_{0}-12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})},

where

g2=(k−2​δ)212,g3=−(k−2​δ)3216−C136,g_{2}=\frac{(k-2\,\delta)^{2}}{12},\quad g_{3}=-\frac{(k-2\,\delta)^{3}}{216}-\frac{C_{1}}{36}, (63)

and Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0. Then the solutions of Eq. (2) can be found from the relation

u⁡(x,t)=2​ca​(U⁡(θ)+δ).u(x,t)=\frac{2\,c}{a}(U(\theta)+\delta). (64)

When we choose C1=0C_{1}=0, the polynomial (62) has two different roots: 00 (with multiplicity two) and U0=−3(k−2δ)/2U_{0}=-3(k-2\,\delta)/2. For the nonzero root we have the following solution

U⁡(θ)=6​℘​(θ+ω,g2,g3)−(k−2​δ)2U(\theta)=6\,\wp(\theta+\omega;g_{2},g_{3})-\frac{(k-2\,\delta)}{2} (65)

where

g2=(k−2​δ)212,g3=−(k−2​δ)3216g_{2}=\frac{(k-2\,\delta)^{2}}{12},\quad g_{3}=-\frac{(k-2\,\delta)^{3}}{216} (66)

with Δ=0\Delta=0. Therefore, we can express the Weierstrass function as hyperbolic (102) and trigonometric (103) forms. Then, substituting U⁡(θ)U(\theta) given by (65) in (64), having in mind the simplified form of the Weierstrass function, and choosing δ=3​k/4\delta=3\,k/4 where k=(1−c)/ck=(1-c)/c, θ=x−c​t\theta=x-c\,t, we have solitary wave (dark soliton) solutions for c>1c>1

u⁡(x,t)=3​(c−1)2​a​tanh2⁡[12​c−12​c​(x−c​t)]u(x,t)=\frac{3(c-1)}{2a}\ \tanh^{2}\left[\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{c-1}{2c}}(x-c\,t)\right]

and periodic singular solutions for c<1c<1

u⁡(x,t)=3​(1−c)2​a​tan2⁡[12​1−c2​c​(x−c​t)].u(x,t)=\frac{3(1-c)}{2a}\ \tan^{2}\left[\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{1-c}{2c}}(x-c\,t)\right].

Here we can also consider the special value δ=0\delta=0. In this case we have

(d​Ud​θ)2=23​U3+k​U2+C1\left(\frac{dU}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{2}{3}U^{3}+k\,U^{2}+C_{1} (67)

and the third order polynomial has three different roots. Taking into account Eq. (98), the solution of (67) for each root takes the form

U=−5​k​U0+4​U02+12​U0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)k+2​U0−12​℘​(θ,g2,g3)U=-\frac{5\,k\,U_{0}+4\,U_{0}^{2}+12\,U_{0}\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{k+2\,U_{0}-12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})} (68)

where

g2=k212,g3=−k3216−C136.g_{2}=\frac{k^{2}}{12},\quad\quad g_{3}=-\frac{k^{3}}{216}-\frac{C_{1}}{36}. (69)

If C1≠0C_{1}\neq 0, the discriminant of g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} is different from zero, and therefore the solutions of Eq. (68) can not be simplified. Since we are interested in solitary wave and periodic solutions, we can choose C1=0C_{1}=0. Then, the invariants take the form of (29) with n=1n=1 and Δ=0\Delta=0. Thus, the third order polynomial has two different roots: 00 (twice) and U0=−3k/2U_{0}=-3k/2. While the root U0=0U_{0}=0 gives the trivial solution of Eq. (67), U=0U=0, the nonzero root implies the following solution

U=3​k4​2​k−12​℘​(θ,g2,g3)k+6​℘​(θ,g2,g3)U=\frac{3k}{4}\ \frac{2k-12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{k+6\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})} (70)

or from (99)

U=6​℘​(θ+ω,g2,g3)−k2U=6\wp(\theta+\omega;g_{2},g_{3})-\frac{k}{2} (71)

where ω\omega is a half period. Now it is easy to check that (70) and (71) correspond to (30) and (31) with n=1n=1, respectively. Therefore, the particular solutions of Eq. (2) can be found substituting n=1n=1 in (36) and (37).

4.2 Modified BBM equation (n=2n=2)

Equation (1) with n=2n=2 reduces to the modified BBM equation (3). Then, Eq. (58) becomes

d2​Ud​θ2−(U3+3​δ​U2+(δ2+k)​U)=0\frac{d^{2}U}{d\theta^{2}}-(U^{3}+3\,\delta\,U^{2}+(\delta^{2}+k)U)=0 (72)

with

D2=−k​δ−δ3.D_{2}=-k\,\delta-\delta^{3}. (73)

To obtain the solution of (72), we have to solve following first order equation that can be seen from the Section 2.3

d​Ud​θ∓12​U4+2​δ​U3+K​U2+C2=0\frac{dU}{d\theta}\mp\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\,U^{4}+2\,\delta\,\,U^{3}+K\,U^{2}+C_{2}}=0 (74)

where K=3​δ2+kK=3\,\delta^{2}+k. For this case we have the forth order polynomial

f⁡(U)=12​U4+2​δ​U3+K​U2+C2f(U)=\frac{1}{2}U^{4}+2\,\delta U^{3}+K\,U^{2}+C_{2} (75)

with four different roots. The solution of Eq. (74) for each root can be obtained, applying the same procedure mentioned above, as

U⁡(θ)=5​K​U0+3​U03+12​δ​U02+12​U0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)12​℘​(θ,g2,g3)−k−3​(δ+U0)2U(\theta)=\frac{5\,K\,U_{0}+3\,U_{0}^{3}+12\,\delta\,U_{0}^{2}+12\,U_{0}\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})-k-3\,(\delta+U_{0})^{2}} (76)

where

g2=K212+C22,g3=−K3216+C2​K12−C2​δ24,g_{2}=\frac{K^{2}}{12}+\frac{C_{2}}{2},\qquad g_{3}=-\frac{K^{3}}{216}+\frac{C_{2}\,K}{12}-\frac{C_{2}\,\delta^{2}}{4}, (77)

and Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0. Now, the solution of Eq. (3) can be obtained from

u⁡(x,t)=3​ca​(U⁡(θ)+δ).u(x,t)=\sqrt{\frac{3\,c}{a}}\,(U(\theta)+\delta). (78)

If C2=0C_{2}=0 and δ≠0\delta\neq 0, the forth order polynomial (75) has three different roots: 00 (with multiplicity two) and

U0±=−2​δ±−2​(k+δ2).U_{0}^{\pm}=-2\,\delta\pm\sqrt{-2\,(k+\delta^{2})}. (79)

In this case Δ=0\Delta=0 and the invariants are

g2=K212,g3=−K3216.g_{2}=\frac{K^{2}}{12},\qquad g_{3}=-\frac{K^{3}}{216}. (80)

When we substitute these roots and the degenerate forms of the Weierstrass function in Eq. (76), we have

U±​(θ)=−2​K2​δ±−2​(k+δ2)​cos​[−K​θ]U^{\pm}(\theta)=\frac{-2\,K}{2\,\delta\pm\sqrt{-2\,(k+\delta^{2})}\,{\rm cos}[\sqrt{-K}\,\theta]}

for c>1c>1, and

U±​(θ)=−2​K2​δ±−2​(k+δ2)​cosh​[K​θ]U^{\pm}(\theta)=\frac{-2\,K}{2\,\delta\pm\sqrt{-2(k+\delta^{2})}\,{\rm cosh}[\sqrt{K}\,\theta]}

for c<1c<1. Therefore, the solution of Eq. (3) can be obtained from (78) considering k=(1−c)/ck=(1-c)/c, θ=x−c​t\theta=x-c\,t.

We can also deal with the case C2≠0C_{2}\neq 0, δ=0\delta=0 and the corresponding forth order polynomial is

f⁡(U)=12​U4+k​U2+C2f(U)=\frac{1}{2}U^{4}+k\,U^{2}+C_{2} (81)

has four different roots:

U0±=±−k−−2​C2+k2U_{0}^{\pm}=\pm\sqrt{-k-\sqrt{-2\,C_{2}+k^{2}}} (82)

and

U0±=±−k+−2​C2+k2.U_{0}^{\pm}=\pm\sqrt{-k+\sqrt{-2\,C_{2}+k^{2}}}. (83)

Substituting (81) in terms of U0U_{0} in Eq. (98), the solution of Eq. (74) with δ=0\delta=0 for each root is

U=−5​k​U0+3​U03+12​U0​℘​(θ,g2,g3)k+3​U02−12​℘​(θ,g2,g3)U=-\frac{5\,k\,U_{0}+3\,U_{0}^{3}+12\,U_{0}\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})}{k+3\,U_{0}^{2}-12\,\wp(\theta;g_{2},g_{3})} (84)

where

g2=k212+C22,g3=−k3216+C2​k12,g_{2}=\frac{k^{2}}{12}+\frac{C_{2}}{2},\qquad g_{3}=-\frac{k^{3}}{216}+\frac{C_{2}\,k}{12}, (85)

and Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0.

Now, it is easy to see that the trivial choice C2=0C_{2}=0 gives rise to the invariants (41) with n=2n=2 and Δ=0\Delta=0. Then we will get the solitary wave and the periodic solutions. The roots (U0U_{0}) also take the forms: 00 (multiplicity two) and U0±=±−2​kU_{0}^{\pm}=\pm\sqrt{-2\,k}. Therefore, the Weierstrass function can be expressed in terms of hyperbolic and trigonometric functions. Then, the solitary wave and trigonometric solutions of Eq. (3) can be read from (36) and (37) with n=2n=2 only for U0±U_{0}^{\pm}.

For this case, we have also another type of solution for certain values of C2=k2/2C_{2}=k^{2}/2 for which we have the special form of (93):

  1. 1.

    If c<1c<1, the equation

    (d​Ud​θ)2=12​(U2+k)2\left(\frac{dU}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(U^{2}+k)^{2} (86)

    has the solution

    U=k​tan⁡[k2​θ].U=\sqrt{k}\,\tan\left[\sqrt{\frac{k}{2}}\,\theta\right]. (87)
  2. 2.

    If c>1c>1, the equation

    (d​Ud​θ)2=12​(U2−(−k))2\left(\frac{dU}{d\theta}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(U^{2}-(-k))^{2} (88)

    has the solution

    U=−k​tanh⁡[−k2​θ].U=\sqrt{-k}\,\tanh\left[\sqrt{\frac{-k}{2}}\,\theta\right]. (89)

Thus, for c<1c<1 the solutions of (1) are periodic singular kink type

u⁡(x,t)=3​(1−c)a​tan⁡[1−c2​c​(x−c​t)]u(x,t)=\sqrt{\frac{3(1-c)}{a}}\,\tan\left[\sqrt{\frac{1-c}{2c}}(x-c\,t)\right]

and for c>1c>1 the solutions are of kink type

u⁡(x,t)=3​(c−1)a​tanh⁡[c−12​c​(x−c​t)].u(x,t)=\sqrt{\frac{3(c-1)}{a}}\ \tanh\left[\sqrt{\frac{c-1}{2c}}(x-c\,t)\right].

5 Conclusions

In this paper we have first factorized the generalized BBM equation in two ways. Then, we have investigated the travelling wave solutions of this equation by means of the factorization technique. We have obtained particular solutions of the generalized BBM as well as general solutions of the modified-BBM and BBM equations in terms of elliptic functions without making any ansatz [4, 5, 6]. We want to stress that this technique is more systematic than others previously used for the analysis of these equations. The factorization technique gives directly solutions of the BBM in terms of elliptic functions. Indeed, we have more general solutions and recovered all the solutions reported in [4, 5, 6]. At the same time we have shown the equivalence of certain expressions that, in fact, describe the same solutions for the BBM equation.

Appendix: Elliptic functions

Let us consider any quartic polynomial

f⁡(φ)=a0​φ4+4​a1​φ3+6​a2​φ2+4​a3​φ+a4f(\varphi)=a_{0}\,\varphi^{4}+4\,a_{1}\,\varphi^{3}+6\,a_{2}\,\varphi^{2}+4\,a_{3}\,\varphi+a_{4} (90)

and the differential equation

(d​φd​t)2=f⁡(φ).\left(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\right)^{2}=f(\varphi). (91)

The simplest case in which Eq. (91) is integrable is when f⁡(φ)f(\varphi) is given by

f⁡(φ)=α02​(α2±φ2)2.f(\varphi)=\alpha_{0}^{2}\,(\alpha^{2}\pm\varphi^{2})^{2}. (92)

Then the corresponding differential equation

(d​φd​t)2=α02​(α2±φ2)2\left(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\right)^{2}=\alpha_{0}^{2}\,(\alpha^{2}\pm\varphi^{2})^{2} (93)

has the solutions

φ−=α​tanh⁡[α​α0​θ]\varphi^{-}=\alpha\,\tanh[\alpha\,\alpha_{0}\,\theta] (94)

and

φ+=α​tan⁡[α​α0​θ].\varphi^{+}=\alpha\,\tan[\alpha\,\alpha_{0}\,\theta]. (95)

In the general case, the invariants of (90) are defined as

g2\displaystyle g_{2} =\displaystyle= a0​a4−4​a1​a3+3​a22,\displaystyle a_{0}\,a_{4}-4\,a_{1}\,a_{3}+3\,a_{2}^{2}, (96)
g3\displaystyle g_{3} =\displaystyle= a0​a2​a4+2​a1​a2​a3−a23−a0​a32−a12​a4,\displaystyle a_{0}\,a_{2}\,a_{4}+2\,a_{1}\,a_{2}\,a_{3}-a_{2}^{3}-a_{0}\,a_{3}^{2}-a_{1}^{2}\,a_{4}, (97)

and the variable z=∫φ0φ[f(t)]−1/2dtz=\int_{\varphi_{0}}^{\varphi}[f(t)]^{-1/2}dt, where φ0\varphi_{0} is any root of the equation f⁡(φ)=0f(\varphi)=0, is introduced. If the Weierstrass function ℘⁡(z,g2,g3)\wp(z;g_{2},g_{3}) is constructed with the help of the invariants g2g_{2} and g3g_{3}, then φ\varphi can be expressed as a rational function of it as

φ=φ0+14​f′​(φ0)​(℘⁡(z,g2,g3)−124​f′′​(φ0))−1,\varphi=\varphi_{0}+\frac{1}{4}f^{\prime}(\varphi_{0})\left(\wp(z;g_{2},g_{3})-\frac{1}{24}f^{\prime\prime}(\varphi_{0})\right)^{-1}, (98)

where the prime (′) denotes the derivative with respect to φ\varphi. We have also the following useful relation for the Weierstrass function (once the invariants are fixed, and we can avoid them to alleviate the notation)

℘⁡(z+ω,g2,g3)=e1+(e1−e2)​(e1−e3)℘⁡(z,g2,g3)−e1\wp(z+\omega;g_{2},g_{3})=e_{1}+\frac{(e_{1}-e_{2})(e_{1}-e_{3})}{\wp(z;g_{2},g_{3})-e_{1}} (99)

where ω\omega is half-period and e1,e2,e3e_{1},\,e_{2},\,e_{3} are roots of the equation 4​t3−g2​t−g3=04t^{3}-g_{2}t-g_{3}=0, such that

e1+e2+e3=0,e1​e2+e1​e3+e2​e3=−14​g2,e1​e2​e3=14​g3.\begin{array}[]{l}e_{1}+e_{2}+e_{3}=0,\\ e_{1}\,e_{2}+e_{1}\,e_{3}+e_{2}\,e_{3}=-\frac{1}{4}g_{2},\\ e_{1}\,e_{2}\,e_{3}=\frac{1}{4}g_{3}.\end{array} (100)

When g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} are real and the discriminant

Δ=g23−27​g32\Delta=g_{2}^{3}-27\,g_{3}^{2} (101)

is positive, negative or zero, we have different behaviors of ℘⁡(z)\wp(z).

Here, we shall discuss the case Δ=0\Delta=0, that corresponds to degenerate cases of the Weierstrass functions which occur when one or both of periods become infinite, or, what is the same, two or all three roots e1,e2,e3e_{1},\,e_{2},\,e_{3} coincide.

If e1=e2=b>0,e3=−2​be_{1}=e_{2}=b>0,\,e_{3}=-2\,b, then g2>0g_{2}>0, g3<0g_{3}<0 and the real and imaginary periods of the Weierstrass function, ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime}, are ω=∞,ω′=iπ(12b)−1/2\omega=\infty,\,\omega^{\prime}=i\pi(12\,b)^{-1/2}, and this function can be written as

℘⁡(z,12​b2,−8​b3)=b+3​b​sinh−2⁡[(3​b)1/2​z],\wp(z;12\,b^{2},-8\,b^{3})=b+3\,b\sinh^{-2}[(3\,b)^{1/2}z], (102)

which leads to solitary wave solutions.

If e1=2​b>0e_{1}=2\,b>0, e2=e3=−be_{2}=e_{3}=-b, then g2>0g_{2}>0, g3>0g_{3}>0, ω=π(12b)−1/2\omega=\pi(12\,b)^{-1/2}, ω′=i​∞\omega^{\prime}=i\infty, and the Weierstrass function becomes

℘⁡(z,12​b2,8​b3)=−b+3​b​sin−2⁡[(3​b)1/2​z],\wp(z;12\,b^{2},8\,b^{3})=-b+3\,b\sin^{-2}[(3\,b)^{1/2}z], (103)

which leads to periodic solutions [10, 11].

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
